candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Non-causal determinism does not establish the consequence argument's conclusion because logical dependence cannot determine causal control or agential sourcehood.
candidates.attributionBasis: The explicit affirmative response at event 1692 begins Hawkins's sustained answer and continues until Folley takes the next marked turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly defends libertarian agency against a determinist argument by separating logical entailment from the causal and practical concepts of control and sourcehood.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's proposal to recast the consequence argument using non-causal determinism.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley asks whether a non-causal version of the consequence argument could coexist with libertarian freedom; Hawkins accepts the picture but rejects its inference from fixed propositions to absent control.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Non-causal determinism offers a stronger and more attractive basis for compatibilism because predictability need not imply causal puppeteering.
candidates.attributionBasis: A marked Folley turn introduces his own compatibilist position and develops it continuously through the discussion of Laplace's demon and predictability.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies the con side's core metaphysical alternative, retaining determinism while removing the causal-compulsion picture that motivates incompatibilist concern.
candidates.contextSummary: After agreeing that logical dependence differs from control, Folley presents non-causal determinism as the foundation of his compatibilism and locates determinism's unsettling force in complete external predictability.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Free will should be understood functionally through the distinctions needed to allocate incentives, prediction, praise, and blame even in a deterministic society.
candidates.attributionBasis: Folley's uninterrupted extended turn develops a thought experiment about deterministic societies, pathological behavior, coercion, prediction, and the practical work performed by freedom concepts.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the central compatibilist-pragmatist case: meaningful freedom survives metaphysical determinism because social and deliberative practices require graded distinctions among kinds of action.
candidates.contextSummary: Folley argues that free will has multiple practical meanings, using punishment, reflexes, premeditated murder, brain tumors, and coercion to show why agents must distinguish behavior by responsiveness and utility.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Agency remains indispensable in practice, and even complete foreknowledge can be passive while actions are still causally attributable to choosing agents.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins takes the marked response turn, explicitly addresses Folley's practical account, and develops the analogy between deterministic physics and divine foreknowledge until Folley intervenes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response absorbs the pragmatic need for responsibility into the pro case while arguing that prediction or foreknowledge does not displace the agent as the source of action.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's functional account of freedom as allocating incentives, praise, blame, and useful behavioral distinctions.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins agrees that society cannot live without agency distinctions, then compares physical prediction with passive divine foreknowledge and argues that deliberation does not treat decisions as predetermined causal links.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Bradleyan idealism accepts scientific truths while rejecting the unsupported naturalist claim that scientific truths exhaust reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: Following Folley's direct invitation, Hawkins gives a sustained exposition of Bradley and British idealism, with stable first-person framing and no competing speaker turn until the endpoint.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This establishes the idealist half of the pro position by challenging reductive naturalism and requiring metaphysics to integrate scientific, moral, aesthetic, religious, and agential experience.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's request for Bradley's beliefs and for an explanation of how his idealism differs from other idealist traditions.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins places British idealism amid nineteenth-century scientific upheaval, accepts scientific discovery, rejects the added exclusivity premise, and presents Bradley's systematic metaphysics of the whole of experience.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Bradley improves on Hegel by treating reality as richer than rational thought, with feeling and volition preceding intellectual systematization.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins explicitly introduces Bradley's rejection of thought-centered Hegelian idealism and carries the same exposition through its contrast with contemporary analytic idealisms.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move identifies the distinctive Bradleyan basis for accommodating agency, value, and aesthetics and explains why intellectual science cannot constitute a complete account of reality.
candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins argues that direct felt engagement precedes rational modeling, uses infant experience as support, and contends that science and philosophy deliberately omit agential, ethical, and aesthetic dimensions.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: A naturalistically acceptable idealism can treat experience as the subject matter and physical stuff as a model constructed from experience.
candidates.attributionBasis: The marked Folley turn uses Carnap, phenomenalism, Hume, and the Vienna Circle to articulate his own experience-first but naturalistic position before Hawkins resumes.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This offers the con side a naturalist-friendly appropriation of idealism, narrowing the dispute by denying that an experience-first ontology requires mysterious mental substances or anti-naturalism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins's presentation of Bradleyan idealism as a broader alternative to reductive and thought-centered accounts.

candidates.contextSummary: After Hawkins affirms Folley's phenomenological reconstruction, Folley distinguishes mental-substance claims from an experience-centered methodology and characterizes physical objects as useful models of experience.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Idealism is philosophically pervasive because inquiry cannot bypass experience and judgment, but Bradley further requires inquiry to move beyond thought and language.
candidates.attributionBasis: Hawkins resumes after Folley's Carnapian account, explicitly agrees before stating his divergence, and continues through the delivered explanation and closing comprehension check.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly contrasts Bradleyan idealism with naturalistic phenomenalism and argues that consciousness, reference, agency, morality, and aesthetics expose the limits of exclusively intellectual explanation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's proposal that experience-first phenomenalism is already a fully naturalistic and metaphysically modest form of idealism.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins argues that the historical anomaly is the attempted leap beyond experience, cites pressures in mind and language, and explains Bradley's interwoven intellectual, moral, aesthetic, and felt modes of engagement.
